note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — ONE WHORL OF LONG SLIM RAYS
tiles.details: Start with CC0 panel 4: trace the thin flowering culm to its main starburst hub and count actual long narrow arms; compare the Cleveland Powell CC BY open-wheel panels 0 and 3, then contrast the developing compressed head in panel 1. The Mexican taxonomic key characterizes C. andropogonoides by generally one radiating whorl and fewer than ten spikelets per centimeter of an attached mature raceme. No image contains a usable true 1-cm measuring scale for that count. Some look-alike Chloris and hybrids overlap, so never certify from arm number or silhouette alone.
tiles.short: Trace the entire flowering axis: many slender radiating racemes from one main whorl.
tiles.status: TRUE ATTACHED HEAD AND ONE-WHORL HUB PHOTOGRAPHED; 1-CM RACEME COUNT MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED BASE, TRUE LIGULE AND COLLAR
tiles.details: The same CC0 exact-source photo (panel 4) shows a thin attached culm, leaf blades and overlapping pale lower sheaths; roots and the true inner blade–sheath ligule are NOT in focus or exposed. Hagenbuch and Lemke's Hill Country key describes a short membranous ligule around 1 mm, truncate/erose and sometimes sparsely ciliate. The next specimen photo must show a truly connected fibrous-root crown and any lower rooting nodes, plus a separately peeled actual blade–sheath junction with a 1-mm scale. Do not label a white lower leaf sheath as a ligule or assert a stolon from the photo.
tiles.short: Find the actual inner membranous ligule, reported up to about 1 mm, not loose collar hairs.
tiles.status: PARTIAL SAME-SHOOT BASAL SHEATH HABIT VISIBLE; ROOTS/TRUE LIGULE UNPHOTOGRAPHED

tiles.heading: 03 · SPIKELET, BOTH GLUMES AND FLORET COUNT
tiles.details: Panels 3 and 2 are REAL attached unilateral narrow flowering branches and panel 0 shows their full hub. Published species treatments describe one rudimentary upper floret, and a useful practical check is fewer than ten mature spikelets per centimeter of the raceme. Neither hand nor finger gives an actual mm scale; zooming these JPEGs cannot establish a measured 1-cm count, glume boundaries or the number of tiny florets. Photograph a true 1-cm segment and separately opened spikelets under 10–20×.
tiles.short: Examine a mature one-sided raceme under 10–20×; separate glumes from the fertile and reduced sterile florets.
tiles.status: VISIBLE ATTACHED RACEMES — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO THREE DISSECTED SPIKELETS

tiles.heading: 04 · FERTILE LEMMA, STERILE LEMMA AND AWNS
tiles.details: The real archived panels illustrate thin rays and the gross bract-covered spikelets only; they do NOT yet resolve fertile versus reduced sterile lemma, actual inserted awns or hairs at millimeter scale. The Mexican botanical treatment describes fertile lemmas around 2–4.6 mm and a reduced sterile lemma around 1–2 × 0.3–0.5 mm. Open one mature labelled same-voucher spikelet, retain both glumes and photograph each lemma and corresponding awn origin separately next to a real mm scale. Never use the different-species C. verticillata macro as proof for this taxon.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma about 2–4.6 mm; single rudimentary sterile lemma about 1–2 × 0.3–0.5 mm.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MICRO-ANATOMY — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO ATTACHMENTS AND SCALE

tiles.heading: 05 · LOCAL WINDMILL LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Panel 4 is actual C. andropogonoides with a single narrow radiating hub and lower sheaths, while panel 5 is a DIFFERENT species (C. virgata, featherier compact head) and panel 6 a DIFFERENT species (C. verticillata, awned reproductive macro). Tumble windmillgrass may bear well-separated branch tiers; hooded windmillgrass C. cucullata has a different inflated sterile lemma. Source literature documents possible intermediates or hybrids; compare mature glumes and lemmas before determining an uncertain plant. No visual panel confirms a particular hybrid.
tiles.short: Separate one-whorl slender rays from tiered whorls, short crowded branches and feathery annual heads.
tiles.status: REAL OTHER-SPECIES COMPARISONS — ANATOMY STILL UNVERIFIED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — TWO EXACT HANDOFFS
tiles.details: CURRENT RECONCILED COVERAGE: six exact-species JPEGs are physically archived (five CC BY or CC0 and one historical CC BY-NC). Five open-license exact-species photos appear in the gallery, with two differently labelled look-alike photo panels. Specific remaining needs: same-voucher exposed rooted base and actual rooting nodes if present; peeled inner membranous ligule with 1-mm ruler; full intact mature single whorl with scale for spikelet count per cm; measured mature opened glumes and fertile/reduced sterile lemmas with separately followed awns; independent rights/source checks and mobile/Pages QA. The old CC BY-NC photo is not automatically illegal on this declared noncommercial site, but its precise individual license version and final rights-filtered policy require independent verification before installation as a gallery panel. No new photographs archived in this pass.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — rooted base and authentic ligule still missing

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: LOOK HERE FIRST: see the broad wheel of long, very slim radiating racemes on the flowering stem. Photograph the WHOLE head, then one branch and a mature spikelet. Many Chloris species make windmills, so the thin radiating silhouette alone supports a candidate, not a certain species ID; compare feather fingergrass and tumble windmillgrass.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: 1 · FIELD HEAD: begin with real source-identified panel 4, which connects one narrow windmill seedhead to its flowering stem, and with panels 0 and 3 for fully spread mature raceme hubs. The two new arrows on panel 3 mark only photographed hub and a long attached raceme.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: The same CC0 exact-source photo (panel 4) shows a thin attached culm, leaf blades and overlapping pale lower sheaths; roots and the true inner blade–sheath ligule are NOT in focus or exposed. Hagenbuch and Lemke's Hill Country key describes a short membranous ligule around 1 mm, truncate/erose and sometimes sparsely ciliate. The next specimen photo must show a truly connected fibrous-root crown and any lower rooting nodes, plus a separately peeled actual blade–sheath junction with a 1-mm scale. Do not label a white lower leaf sheath as a ligule or assert a stolon from the photo.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Panels 3 and 2 are REAL attached unilateral narrow flowering branches and panel 0 shows their full hub. Published species treatments describe one rudimentary upper floret, and a useful practical check is fewer than ten mature spikelets per centimeter of the raceme. Neither hand nor finger gives an actual mm scale; zooming these JPEGs cannot establish a measured 1-cm count, glume boundaries or the number of tiny florets. Photograph a true 1-cm segment and separately opened spikelets under 10–20×.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Compared with feather fingergrass, the existing slimspike photo shows relatively hair-thin, less obviously feathery rays. Tumble windmillgrass is particularly suggested by multiple vertically separated raceme tiers, not simply a large wheel. Species-level certainty requires mature spikelet and lemma details that this one source photo does not provide.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: SAME FLOWERING SHOOT — seedhead, leaves and lower sheaths
panels.caption: One species-source-identified flowering shoot is visible from the thin terminal starburst through the straight culm to several green narrow leaves and overlapping pale lower sheaths held over the hand. Two arrows mark the photographed head hub and lower sheath cluster. This is NOT a confirmed ROOTED crown photo: soil connection, fibrous roots, a spreading stolon, and any true free ligule edge remain outside visible pixels. It cannot prove perennial life cycle or separated rooted nodes.
panels.creator: no rights reserved
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE / PARENT: Chloris virgata
panels.caption: Different species: the close terminal feathery fan of feather fingergrass is noticeably fuller than the hand-held slim-rayed source photograph.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: COMPARE TUMBLE WINDMILLGRASS — genuine awned spikelet close-up (OTHER species)
panels.caption: This is TUMBLE WINDMILLGRASS (C. verticillata), not slimspike. Look closely at the photographed awned spikelet and a projecting awn. Its true glumes, sterile lemma shape and awn lengths are not individually resolved or calibrated. Do not transfer any of these details to C. andropogonoides just because their windmill heads resemble each other.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.
